subject: Agriculture
title: The Aral Sea Disaster
description: A quick, practical guide to The Aral Sea Disaster.

hook.text: The Aral Sea was the world's fourth-largest lake. Then the Soviet Union diverted its rivers for cotton.

buildup.text: Starting in the 1960s, canals redirected the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate desert cotton fields.

discovery.text: Without inflow, the Aral Sea shrank by 90%. Fishing towns sat stranded, miles from any water.

twist.text: Exposed lakebed created toxic dust storms. Salt and pesticide residue blew across farms and villages.

climax.text: NASA calls it one of the worst environmental disasters in history. The sea is now mostly desert.

punchline.text: They grew cotton. They lost a sea.

quiz.question: What caused the Aral Sea to shrink by 90%?
options: Rivers feeding it were diverted for cotton irrigation

details.summary: The Aral Sea disaster is one of the worst environmental catastrophes in modern history, caused by Soviet irrigation diversions that drained what was once the world's fourth-largest lake. This topic covers the decisions that destroyed it, the ecological fallout, and partial restoration efforts.
details.whyItMatters: The Aral Sea's destruction is the most dramatic example of irrigation gone wrong. It shows how unsustainable water diversion can devastate ecosystems, economies, and the health of millions of people.
takeaways: Soviet cotton irrigation diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers from the Aral Sea
The sea lost 90% of its volume, splitting into fragments and leaving toxic salt flats
A dam project partially restored the North Aral Sea, bringing back fish and fisheries

faq.question: What caused the Aral Sea to shrink so dramatically?
faq.answer: Starting in the 1960s, the Soviet Union diverted the two rivers feeding the Aral Sea to irrigate cotton fields in Central Asia. Deprived of inflow, the sea steadily evaporated, losing 90% of its volume by the 2000s.

faq.question: Has anything been done to restore the Aral Sea?
faq.answer: Kazakhstan built the Kok-Aral Dam in 2005 to save the North Aral Sea, raising water levels and restoring fisheries. However, the South Aral Sea remains mostly dry and recovery prospects are poor without fundamentally changing irrigation practices.
